claims.text: The starting material is a nanoscale multilayer coating composed of FCC and BCC high-entropy alloys.
The baseline interfaces have relatively disordered chemistry.
The baseline FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer has significant lattice distortion.
Deposition temperature and interlayer composition will be systematically varied as the experimental intervention.
Changing deposition temperature and interlayer composition can enhance interfacial chemical short-range order.
The comparison will use sustained loading under controlled temperature and stress.
Stronger local chemical ordering reduces local lattice distortion.
The order–distortion relationship controls dislocation mobility.
Enhancing interfacial chemical order reduces local lattice-distortion barriers in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
Reduced lattice distortion facilitates more efficient dislocation transmission across FCC/BCC interfaces.
Enhanced interfacial ordering shifts the dominant creep mechanism from dislocation climb to interface-mediated plasticity.
The interface-mediated mechanism may involve twin nucleation and development.
More strongly ordered interfaces will produce lower creep strain rates than uncontrolled interfaces.
More strongly ordered interfaces will produce modified dislocation patterns relative to the baseline.
More strongly ordered interfaces may increase twin-related activity relative to the baseline.
Standard deposition conditions produce disordered interfaces with greater lattice distortion.
The proposed effect is limited to conditions that preserve the nanoscale multilayer architecture and FCC/BCC phase stability.
The quantitative relationship between chemical ordering and the creep-mechanism shift is uncertain because several deformation modes may overlap.
Interfacial ordering can be quantified by atom-probe tomography while deformation is monitored by TEM and in-situ microscopy.
The hypothesis is falsified if increased ordering produces neither a systematic creep-rate reduction nor a shift away from climb-dominated creep.
